title: Regional Airlines 9288
summary: On approach to Varandey Airport, the crew allowed the aircraft's speed to drop and its nose to rise until it stalled. The airspeed and angle-of-attack indicators may have malfunctioned, making it difficult for the crew to monitor flight parameters accurately.

title: Tuninter 1153
summary: Tuninter Flight 1153 ditched in the Mediterranean Sea after both engines failed due to fuel exhaustion. The right engine failed at 23,000 feet and the left engine failed 100 seconds later at 21,900 feet. The cause was an incorrect fuel quantity indicator designed for the ATR 42 installed on the ATR 72, causing ground crews to load insufficient fuel. The crew could not recognize fuel exhaustion because the gauge showed adequate fuel even after all usable fuel was consumed.
probable_cause: Fuel exhaustion caused by installation of an ATR 42 fuel quantity indicator on the ATR 72, resulting in inadequate fuel loading and crew inability to detect the fuel depletion.

title: Copterline 103
summary: Flight 103 departed Tallinn at 12:45 local time on 10 August 2005 bound for Helsinki. Three to five minutes after takeoff at approximately 500 m altitude, the helicopter suddenly lost its steerability and plunged into the sea. Investigation revealed the hydraulic flight control system failed due to plasma coating flakes from servo pistons blocking return valves. All 14 occupants drowned as the emergency floats did not inflate in time.
probable_cause: Failure of the hydraulic flight control system caused by coating flaking off from servo pistons, blocking return valves and causing abrupt loss of maneuverability. Copterline was criticized for omitting required servicing of these components.

title: Helios Airways 522

agencies.name: Air Accident Investigation and Aviation Safety Board

summary: Boeing 737-300 departed Larnaca with the cabin pressurization system mistakenly set to manual mode by a ground engineer who had performed a pressurization leak check but failed to reset it to auto mode afterward. The flight crew overlooked this incorrect setting during the preflight procedure, after-start check and after-takeoff check. As the aircraft climbed through 12,040 feet the cabin altitude warning horn sounded but was misidentified by the crew as a takeoff configuration warning which has an identical alert sound. The aircraft continued climbing while cabin pressure gradually decreased causing critical hypoxia of all occupants.
probable_cause: Cabin pressurization system was left on manual by ground engineer and not reset. Flight crew failed to detect the incorrect setting during three separate preflight checks. Aircraft climbed while cabin depressurized causing critical hypoxia.

title: West Caribbean Airways 708

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety

summary: While cruising at 33,000 feet, West Caribbean Airways 708 experienced gradual airspeed decay and entered an aerodynamic stall. The captain, misinterpreting an engine thrust reduction from the activated anti-icing system as a double engine flameout, failed to recognize and recover from the stall despite the first officer's correct diagnosis. The aircraft crashed in northern Venezuela with all 160 people on board killed.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from pilot error in the failure to recognize and recover from an aerodynamic stall caused by inadequate airspeed monitoring during autopilot level flight in icing conditions, combined with misdiagnosis of engine behavior and inadequate crew coordination.

factors.evidence: The aircraft's speed gradually decreased until it entered an aerodynamic stall.
The captain probably believed they were dealing with an engine flameout and did not recognize the stall.
The autopilot had already compensated with a nose-up attitude even allowing the speed to continue to drop towards a stall situation, without sending a warning or disconnecting.
Although the first officer correctly diagnosed the situation as a stall and attempted twice to communicate this to the captain, the captain did not recognize it.
The captain was confused by the unusual behavior of the engines due to the anti-ice system and probably the airflow disruption.
The aircraft was already approaching a stall condition in severe thunderstorms and was pummeled by sudden turbulence.
West Caribbean had received an operation bulletin warning of autopilot behavior but had not shared this bulletin with its pilots.

West Caribbean had received an operation bulletin from the plane's manufacturer three years earlier, warning that the autopilot could try to compensate for inadequate speed, but had not shared this with pilots.

title: TANS Perú 204
summary: Boeing 737 attempted approach to Pucallpa during developing unusual cold front with cloud tops at 45,000 feet, torrential rain, hail, and strong winds. Aircraft flew through hailstorm in final 32 seconds of flight, taken down by wind shear, struck tree tops and impacted swamp 3.8 nautical miles ahead of runway threshold. Investigation attributed pilot error to failing to divert when weather deteriorated and inadequate instrument monitoring.
probable_cause: Pilot error for not following standard procedures under adverse weather conditions; failure to divert when weather was obviously unsuitable; crew did not notice rapid descent in critical final seconds.

title: Mandala Airlines 091
summary: Mandala Airlines Flight 091 crashed into a residential area seconds after taking off from Polonia International Airport on September 5, 2005. The flight crew did not configure the aircraft properly for takeoff with flaps and slats retracted. The retracted flaps and slats resulted in the aircraft being unable to fly due to insufficient lift. The aircraft stalled and veered left and right, with the tail impacting the runway before crashing into the road. Of 117 on board, only 17 survived and 49 civilians on the ground were killed.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by the actions of the flight crew in that they did not configure the aircraft properly for takeoff. The retracted flaps and slats resulted in the aircraft being unable to fly due to insufficient lift. The takeoff warning was not heard and pilots may not have been aware of their erroneous actions.

title: Bellview Airlines 210
summary: Boeing 737-200 was a 24-year-old aircraft that had logged more than 55,000 flight hours at the time of the crash. While in Accra, the crews had a discussion on the low pressure reading of the brake accumulator system at approximately 650 psi, significantly lower than its normal value of 1000 psi. The issue was discussed by engineers and maintenance crews who tried to troubleshoot by verifying against another Bellview Airlines Boeing 737. A faulty brake accumulator was later discovered but the aircraft was deemed within safe operation limits and allowed to fly from Lagos to Abuja. On 22 October 2005, Flight 210 took off at 7:30 p.m. and nose-dived and crashed at high speed a few minutes after takeoff, killing all 117 people on board.
probable_cause: Cause could not be determined due to lack of flight data recorders and evidence. The brake accumulator pressure issue was identified but not resolved before flight. Aircraft impacted at nearly vertical angle at approximately 400 knots.

title: Chalk's Ocean Airways 101
summary: Shortly after takeoff from Miami Seaplane Base, white smoke appeared and the right wing separated from the fuselage, causing the 58-year-old aircraft to plunge into the ocean. The fatigue crack had been detected and repaired previously, but the repair was ineffective. The operator applied sealant over the damaged lower stringer, concealing a fatigue crack that had been ground out in an earlier failed repair attempt.
probable_cause: A fatigue failure in the right-wing initiated by a crack in a span-wise stringer close to the wing root. The crack had been detected and seemingly repaired, but the repair was ineffective. Chalk's maintenance program was ineffective at addressing longstanding structural problems.
